group_assessment.weighting: Retrospective single-centre cohort of 852 adults (median age 67) in an emergency department with plasma sodium at or below 125 mmol/L, with chart review of symptoms and blinded radiologist re-reads of imaging, outcome rates of cerebral edema (4) and osmotic demyelination (11). The reported fact is event frequencies in hospital-presenting hyponatremia, mostly chronic, with a stated underpowered, partly imaging-limited design. It is a class-level reference for hypotonic-state brain edema and for correction-rate risk, in adults with common etiologies; not children, not encephalopathy or WWOX, and not a fluid-volume or dextrose intervention study.

entries.proposition: Retrospective single-centre cohort of adults presenting to an emergency department over six years with plasma sodium at or below 125 mmol/L.
entries.snippet: We included patients with age ≥ 18 years and a plasma sodium concentration ≤ 125 mmol/L in the initial blood sample obtained upon admission to the ED.

entries.proposition: The text says 1101 patients had an initial sodium at or below 125 mmol/L; the flow diagram's electronic exclusion of 100,549 patients with sodium above 125 leaves 1,053 of 101,602.
entries.snippet: 1101 patients had an initial plasma sodium ≤ 125 mmol/L and 852 patients were included in this analysis (Figure 1).

entries.proposition: The flow diagram (called Figure 1 in the text; the image file is g002) lists: 101,602 with a sodium; 100,738 excluded electronically, of which 100,549 had sodium above 125; 864 eligible; 12 excluded manually; 852 analysed; 318 severe symptoms (132 imaged), 534 other (67 imaged).
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of the patient flow diagram (image ACEM-33-0-g002): excluded electronically n = 100,738 with initial plasma sodium > 125 mmol/L (n = 100,549), age < 18 (n = 3), blood glucose > 300 (n = 80), missing sodium follow-up (n = 106); eligible n = 864; excluded manually n = 12; primary analysis group n = 852; severe symptoms 318, emergency imaging 132; no or moderate symptoms 534, emergency imaging 67.

experimental_context.system: adult emergency department patients, single centre, 2013-2018

entries.qualifies_needle: 1101 patients had an initial plasma sodium

entries.proposition: Cerebral edema attributable to hyponatremia was confirmed in four patients, 0.5% of 852 and 1.3% of those with severe symptoms.
entries.snippet: Taken together, confirmed hyponatremia‐induced cerebral edema was found in four patients, which represents 0.5% of the primary analysis group and 1.3% of the patients with severe symptoms.

entries.proposition: One of three imaged cases was a 28-year-old woman after MDMA and excessive water drinking with sodium 111 mmol/L who survived 17 days; the same description matches confirmed ODS patient 10 (sodium rise 25 mmol/L in 24 h), not cross-referenced in the text.
entries.snippet: Seizure followed by coma. Had been partying for 2 days, ingestion of high‐volume fluids (urinary osmolality: 58 mOsm/kg). [Na+] 111 mmol/L

entries.proposition: Confirmed ODS in 11 patients (1.3%); overly rapid correction at 24 h was present in seven.
entries.snippet: Seven of the 11 patients with confirmed ODS had well‐established risk factors for ODS, and overly rapid sodium correction at 24 h was also confirmed in seven patients.
entries.anchor: Results, Risk Factors for Development of ODS

entries.proposition: The ODS table row 11 (65-year-old woman, sodium 113 mmol/L, rise 10.1 mmol/L) carries the etiology label of a tea-and-toast diet; row 10 is the water-drinking case; both are low-solute or high-water exposures.
entries.snippet: No No No No 11 65 f 113 10.1 No Yes

entries.proposition: In the primary model overly rapid correction was not associated with ODS (OR 1.65, p 0.219); in the 475-patient sensitivity set it was (OR 4.20, p 0.004).
entries.snippet: overly rapid correction at 24 h was revealed the most important risk factor for ODS (p = 0.004)
entries.anchor: Results, Risk Factors for Development of ODS

entries.proposition: The authors say overly rapid correction occurred in 341 patients (40%), the majority of whom received 5% dextrose; the sentence does not say whether dextrose caused or followed the overcorrection.
entries.snippet: Overly rapid sodium correction occurred in 341 patients (40%), the majority of which received 5% dextrose

entries.proposition: Severe symptoms were frequently accompanied by other brain pathology on imaging (about 38%).
entries.snippet: Of note, imaging studies revealed other pathological findings in a total of 50 patients (37.9%) of the severe symptom group

entries.proposition: The Limitations section says the study is underpowered, few imaged, true incidences likely higher, and that the 24 h sodium was extrapolated.
entries.snippet: Given the small sample size and—even more important—the limited number of imaging studies, our single‐center study is underpowered to draw generalizable conclusions.

entries.proposition: The conclusion is that treatment limits on sodium rise should stay until more evidence exists; it applies to adults with sodium at or below 125 mmol/L, not to mild-moderate hyponatremia.
entries.snippet: Finally, since we only included patients with initial sodium ≤ 125 mmol/L, no recommendations for patients with mild‐to‐moderate hyponatremia can be deduced from our study.
